A PASSION FOR CHOCOLATE
by Catherine Needham

Mother

Eden Vale

If, like me you are a chocolate addict and could live on it indefinitely, you will probably include it in your cooking whenever possible. But, have you ever wondered why chocolate became so popular?

brief_context: Brought cocoa beans from the New World to Europe.
brief_extract:
Drinking chocolate
Chocolate as a confection is a fairly modern preparation but drinking chocolate was known to the people of Central and South Africa many centuries ago. Columbus brought cocoa beans from the New World to Europe. Hernando Cortes, a Spanish soldier, travelled to Mexico and found that the Emperor drank nothing but 'chocolat' — a drink flavoured with vanilla and spices, the thickness of honey, which melted in the mouth.

title: Sir
brief_context: Gave a speech on energy constraints and global resources.
brief_extract:
'WASTE NOT, WANT NOT'

Ann McMullan, EAW Director,
considers:

Might the simple nursery maxim 'Waste not, want not' point the way to a dramatic restructuring of our civilisation? THIS could well be the case if one ponders the implications of a remarkable speech made shortly before Christmas by Sir Monty Finniston to members of the Electrical Industries Club. His far-sighted viewpoint focused far beyond the contemporary wrangling over energy sources and systems, upon the stark realities of constraints inherent in the whole future of global energy.

title: President
brief_context: Mentioned regarding policies for automobile fuel consumption in USA.
brief_extract: Indeed, we are now seeing the first glimmerings of a non-wasteful society, both here and in the USA. There, for instance, President Carter's policies are likely to result in a positive revolution in automobile fuel consumption by 1982 and similar economy planning is in train for the UK too. Listening to Sir Monty, one was suddenly made aware of basic statistics on a global scale.

brief_context: Author of 'Paradise Lost', which was quoted by Finniston.
brief_extract:
He emphasised too that the USA uses 25 per cent of the world's energy supplies when it constitutes only 6 per cent of the world's total population. It was easy to perceive from such figures that the world is 'in a pretty pickle', as Sir Monty himself put it, thus making it clear why he had chosen as the title for his talk 'Confusion, worse confounded' — a particularly apposite quotation from Milton's 'Paradise Lost'. Necessary changes
Sir Monty concluded by reviewing probable or possible trends and patterns.

title: Sir
brief_context: His words are being reflected upon regarding energy consensus.
brief_extract:
Consensus on energy
Reflecting upon Sir Monty’s words, one can perhaps find the possibilities of a realistic energy consensus, for conservationist interests have for long cried out against the squandering society. Indeed, it could well be that the continual proliferation of wasteful practices may in the long run prove far more disastrous for mankind than the proliferation of nuclear weapons.

title: Sir
brief_context: Believes it may be too late to avoid energy difficulties.
brief_extract: Indeed, it is already late in the day, for the nuclear power plant programme will take at least ten years to put into effect and the re-education of our wasteful society is bound to take very much longer. Sir Monty Finniston believes that it may already be too late for us to avoid great difficulties, especially as the educational process is such a slow one. Industry will have to carry out drastic restructuring of long-established patterns and techniques; and such processes could well outspan the short time left to us before a global energy famine could strike.
